title: Stack
description: LIFO structure powering expression evaluation, monotonic patterns, and nested structure parsing. Stacks turn O(n²) brute force into O(n) by maintaining invariants about 'what's still relevant'.

patterns.name: Matching / Balancing
patterns.description: Push opening tokens, pop on matching close. The stack naturally handles nesting depth. Foundation for parsers and compilers.

patterns.name: Monotonic Stack (Decreasing)
patterns.description: Maintain a stack where elements are in decreasing order. When a larger element arrives, pop smaller ones — each pop resolves a 'next greater element' query. O(n) total.

patterns.name: Monotonic Stack (Application-Specific)
patterns.description: Adapt monotonic stack to specific constraints — collision physics, fleet merging, or frequency tracking.

patterns.name: Simulation / State Tracking
patterns.description: Use stack to simulate processes with undo/cancel semantics. Each push is an action, each pop is a reversal.

patterns.name: Stack ↔ Queue Duality
patterns.description: Implement one using the other. Understand amortized costs of the two-stack queue and the lazy transfer technique.

patterns.name: Auxiliary Stack (Min/Max/Freq Tracking)
patterns.description: Maintain a parallel stack tracking metadata (min, max, frequency) at each level. Enables O(1) queries on stack state.

patterns.name: Expression Evaluation
patterns.description: Evaluate postfix, infix, or encoded expressions using operand/operator stacks. Foundation for calculator and compiler problems.

problems.title: Baseball Game
problems.tldr: Simulate a score record with operations: number (add score), '+' (sum of last two), 'D' (double last), 'C' (invalidate last). Stack tracks valid scores — push for add, pop for cancel.
problems.keyTrick: The stack IS the valid score record. 'C' = pop (undo last). 'D' = push(peek * 2). '+' = push(peek + secondFromTop). Numbers = push. Final answer = sum of stack.

approaches.name: Stack Simulation
approaches.description: Process each operation: push scores, pop on 'C', peek for 'D' and '+'. Sum remaining stack.

quiz.q: Why is a stack the natural data structure here (not an array with index)?
options: 'C' invalidates the LAST valid score (LIFO). Stack's pop directly models this undo semantic without index tracking
quiz.explanation: The 'C' operation is precisely stack.pop(). With an array, you'd need to track a 'current end' pointer — essentially reimplementing a stack. Use the right abstraction.

quiz.q: For the '+' operation, how do you access the second-to-last element?
options: Pop the top, peek the new top, compute sum, push the popped value back, then push the sum
Use stack.get(size-2) if available, or pop/push pattern. In Java, LinkedList-based stack allows get()
quiz.explanation: In Java, Stack extends Vector so stack.get(size()-2) works. In a pure stack, pop-peek-push is needed. Know your language's stack implementation details.

quiz.q: What's the time complexity of summing the final stack?
options: O(n) — iterate through remaining elements. Total algorithm is O(n) since each element is pushed/popped at most once
quiz.explanation: Each of the n operations does O(1) work. Final summation is O(n). Total: O(n). The stack ensures no element is processed more than a constant number of times.

quiz.q: How would you extend this to support an 'undo last k operations' command?
options: Maintain a separate operations log (command pattern). To undo k, replay the log without the last k operations
quiz.explanation: This is the Command Pattern from design patterns. Store each operation as a reversible command. Undo = apply inverse commands. This bridges DSA to software design.

quiz.q: This problem is a warm-up. What harder problem uses the same simulation-with-undo pattern?
options: Asteroid Collision — objects interact and cancel each other, requiring stack-based simulation with conditional removal
quiz.explanation: Asteroid Collision is the 'hard mode' of stack simulation — objects don't just cancel; they interact based on direction and size. Same push/pop pattern, more complex conditions.

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.tldr: Check if brackets are balanced: (), {}, []. Push opening brackets. On closing bracket, check if top matches. Stack must be empty at end.
problems.keyTrick: Push opening brackets. On closing bracket: if stack is empty or top doesn't match → invalid. Pop on match. At end, stack must be empty. Pro tip: push the EXPECTED closing bracket instead — then just check top == current.

approaches.name: Stack Matching
approaches.description: Push openers. On closer, verify match with top and pop. Check empty at end.

approaches.name: Push Expected Closer (Cleaner)
approaches.description: On '(' push ')', on '{' push '}', etc. On closer, check if top == current char. Eliminates mapping logic.

quiz.q: Why push the expected closing bracket instead of the opening one?
options: Eliminates the need for a mapping function during comparison. Instead of 'if top is ( and current is )' you just check 'top == current'
quiz.explanation: Pushing the expected closer simplifies the comparison to a single equality check. Less code, fewer bugs. This is the 'elegant' implementation Google interviewers appreciate.

quiz.q: What are the three distinct failure cases?
options: 1) Closer with empty stack (extra closer). 2) Closer doesn't match top (wrong type). 3) Stack non-empty at end (extra opener)
quiz.explanation: Three failure modes: unmatched closer, wrong bracket type, unmatched opener. Each requires a different check. Missing any one is a bug. Test: '(()', ')(', '([)]'.

quiz.q: How does this extend to validating HTML/XML tags?
options: Same pattern: push opening tags, pop on matching closing tags. Tags are strings instead of single chars, but the logic is identical
quiz.explanation: HTML/XML validation is this problem with string tokens instead of characters. Browsers use this stack-based approach for DOM parsing. Real-world application of the same pattern.

quiz.q: What optimization avoids processing strings that are obviously invalid?
options: If string length is odd, return false immediately — valid brackets always come in pairs
quiz.explanation: Odd-length strings can never be balanced. This O(1) check eliminates half of random inputs. Early termination optimizations show attention to detail in interviews.

quiz.q: How is this pattern used in compiler design?
options: Compilers use stack-based parsing for nested expressions, scope resolution, and syntax validation. This is the foundation of recursive descent and shift-reduce parsers
quiz.explanation: Every compiler uses this pattern. Scope nesting (functions inside functions), expression parsing, and syntax validation all use stack-based matching. This is CS fundamentals.

problems.title: Implement Stack Using Queues
problems.tldr: Implement LIFO using FIFO queues. On push: add to queue, then rotate all previous elements behind it (dequeue and re-enqueue n-1 times). This makes pop/top O(1).
problems.keyTrick: Make push expensive: after adding new element, rotate the queue (dequeue and re-enqueue n-1 elements) so the new element is at the front. Now pop and top are O(1). Alternatively, make pop expensive with two queues.

approaches.name: One Queue — Expensive Push
approaches.description: Push: add element, then rotate n-1 times. The newest element stays at front. Pop/top are O(1).

approaches.name: Two Queues — Expensive Pop
approaches.description: Push to q1. Pop: move all but last from q1 to q2, return last. Swap q1/q2.

quiz.q: Why does rotating the queue after push make it behave like a stack?
options: Rotation moves all old elements behind the new one. The queue's front always has the most recently pushed element — LIFO order
quiz.explanation: After push(x) and rotation: queue = [x, prev_top, prev_second, ...]. Front = most recent = LIFO. The rotation transforms FIFO order to LIFO order at each push.

quiz.q: When would the two-queue approach be preferred?
options: When pushes are much more frequent than pops — O(1) push amortizes better in write-heavy workloads
quiz.explanation: If push:pop ratio is high, cheap push (two-queue, pop-expensive) is better. If pop-heavy, cheap pop (one-queue, push-expensive) wins. Match the approach to the workload.

quiz.q: What's the real-world purpose of this exercise?
options: Teaches data structure interconversion, amortized analysis, and the fundamental difference between LIFO and FIFO. Also appears in systems with only queue primitives
quiz.explanation: Some systems (message queues, hardware) only provide FIFO. Knowing how to simulate LIFO from FIFO (and vice versa) is practical. Also tests understanding of abstract data types.

quiz.q: Can you implement a stack using ONE queue without the rotation trick?
options: Not with O(1) pop — you always need some form of reordering. The rotation is the minimal way to achieve LIFO from FIFO
quiz.explanation: A queue only gives access to the front. To get LIFO behavior, you must somehow make the back accessible. Rotation (or n-1 transfers) is the only way with a single queue.

quiz.q: How does this compare to implementing a queue using stacks (the reverse problem)?
options: Queue-from-stacks has an elegant amortized O(1) solution using lazy transfer. Stack-from-queues has no amortized improvement — one operation must always be O(n)
quiz.explanation: Queue-from-stacks achieves amortized O(1) for all operations via lazy reversal. Stack-from-queues cannot — one of push/pop must be O(n). This asymmetry is worth knowing.

problems.title: Implement Queue using Stacks
problems.tldr: Implement FIFO using two LIFO stacks. Push to input stack. Pop/peek: if output stack is empty, transfer ALL from input to output (reverses order). Amortized O(1) per operation.
problems.keyTrick: Lazy transfer: only move elements from input→output when output is empty. The transfer reverses order (LIFO→FIFO). Each element is moved exactly twice (push to input, transfer to output), so amortized O(1).

approaches.name: Two Stacks — Lazy Transfer
approaches.complexity: Amortized O(1) per operation, O(n) space
approaches.description: Push to inStack. On pop/peek, if outStack empty, pour all from inStack to outStack. Pop from outStack.

quiz.q: Why is the amortized cost O(1) even though transfer is O(n)?
options: Each element is pushed to inStack once and transferred to outStack once — exactly 2 moves per element total. Over n operations, total work is O(n), so amortized O(1) per op
quiz.explanation: Amortized analysis: assign each element a 'cost budget' of 2 (one push, one transfer). The expensive O(n) transfer is 'pre-paid' by the n cheap pushes. Banker's method proves this.

quiz.q: What happens if you transfer on EVERY pop instead of only when outStack is empty?
options: Operations degrade to O(n) each. The 'lazy' part is critical — only transfer when necessary to maintain amortized O(1)
quiz.explanation: Eager transfer on every pop means n elements move on every pop = O(n) per pop. Lazy transfer batches the work: one O(n) transfer serves multiple subsequent O(1) pops.

quiz.q: This is used in which real-world system?
options: Functional programming languages implement persistent queues using two stacks. Also used in BFS implementations where only stack primitives are available
quiz.explanation: Purely functional queues (Okasaki's design) use two lists (conceptually stacks). Haskell and Clojure use variants of this. It's a fundamental functional data structure technique.

quiz.q: What's the worst-case (non-amortized) time for a single pop?
options: O(n) — when outStack is empty and all n elements must transfer from inStack. But this only happens after n pushes, so amortized is O(1)
quiz.explanation: Worst case is O(n) for one pop, but this can't happen twice in a row (outStack would have elements after transfer). Understanding worst-case vs amortized is key for Google.

quiz.q: How would you implement a thread-safe version of this?
options: Lock both stacks during transfer to prevent race conditions. Or use lock-free CAS operations. The transfer must be atomic to maintain consistency
quiz.explanation: Concurrent access during transfer could corrupt state. Solutions: mutex around the transfer check, or use a lock-free design with CAS. This bridges to systems design.

problems.title: Min Stack
problems.tldr: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and getMin — all in O(1). Maintain a parallel min-stack where each entry records the minimum at that stack depth.
problems.keyTrick: Push to the min-stack only when new value ≤ current min. Pop from min-stack only when popped value equals current min. This optimization reduces min-stack size. Alternative: store (value, currentMin) pairs on one stack.

approaches.name: Two Stacks (Main + Min)
approaches.description: Main stack for values. Min stack tracks minimum at each level. Push to min when new value ≤ minStack.top.

approaches.name: Single Stack with Pairs
approaches.description: Each stack entry stores (value, minSoFar). Slightly more space but simpler logic.

approaches.name: Encoding Trick (No Extra Stack)
approaches.complexity: O(1) all operations, O(1) extra space
approaches.description: Store (2*val - min) when val < min. Decode on pop. Clever but fragile with integer overflow.

quiz.q: Why must the min-stack push when value EQUALS current min (not just less than)?
options: If the same minimum value is pushed twice and you only track it once, popping one copy would incorrectly remove the min. Duplicates must be counted
quiz.explanation: Push [0, 1, 0]. Min stack: [0, 0]. Pop → removes 0, min stack pops to [0], min is still 0. If we'd only pushed once: min stack = [0], after pop it's empty → wrong min.

quiz.q: What's the space optimization of the conditional push vs always pushing to min-stack?
options: Conditional push only adds to min-stack when a new min (or equal) appears — saves space when values are increasing. Worst case is still O(n) for decreasing sequences
quiz.explanation: For increasing sequences like [1,2,3,...n], min-stack only has [1] vs [1,1,1,...1] with always-push. Average case saves significant space. Worst case (decreasing) is same.

quiz.q: The encoding trick stores (2*val - min) when val < min. Why does this work?
options: When val < min, the encoded value is negative (since val < min → 2*val - min < val). On pop, if encoded < min, we know the real value = min, and previous min = 2*min - encoded
quiz.explanation: The encoding stores the 'delta' from the minimum. When encoded < currentMin, it signals that the currentMin was set by this push. We can reverse-engineer the previous min. Elegant but overflow-prone.

quiz.q: How does Min Stack extend to Max Stack (with popMax)?
options: Max Stack is MUCH harder — popMax requires removing an element from the middle. Use a doubly-linked list + TreeMap for O(log n) popMax. No simple O(1) solution exists
Just track max instead of min
quiz.explanation: Max Stack with popMax is LC 716 (Hard). popMax requires removing a non-top element, breaking stack structure. Doubly-linked list + heap/TreeMap is needed. Very different problem.

quiz.q: In a Google interview, what system design concept does Min Stack illustrate?
options: Metadata tracking alongside data — like database indexes, file system metadata, or cache eviction tracking that maintain invariants with O(1) overhead
quiz.explanation: Maintaining auxiliary metadata (min/max/count) alongside primary data is universal: database indexes, LRU cache freq counts, system monitoring. Min Stack is the simplest form of this pattern.

problems.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
problems.tldr: Evaluate postfix expression. Push numbers onto stack. On operator, pop two operands, apply operator, push result. Final stack element is the answer.
problems.keyTrick: Operand stack: push numbers. On operator: pop b (top), pop a (second), push (a op b). ORDER MATTERS for subtraction and division: a is the first operand, b is the second. Don't swap them.

approaches.name: Stack Evaluation
approaches.description: Single pass: push numbers, on operator pop two operands and push result. Stack depth at most n/2.

quiz.q: Why does the order of operands matter when popping?
options: For subtraction and division, a-b ≠ b-a. The first popped element is b (right operand), second popped is a (left operand). Reversing gives wrong results
quiz.explanation: '4 13 5 / +' means 4 + (13/5). Pop 5 (b), pop 13 (a), compute 13/5=2. If reversed: 5/13=0. This is the #1 bug in RPN implementations.

quiz.q: Why is Reverse Polish Notation used in calculators and some programming languages?
options: No parentheses needed, no operator precedence rules, evaluated in single left-to-right pass. Simpler to parse and evaluate than infix notation
quiz.explanation: RPN eliminates ambiguity: no parentheses, no precedence rules. Stack-based evaluation is O(n) with no lookahead. HP calculators, Forth language, and PostScript all use it.

quiz.q: How would you convert infix to postfix (Shunting-yard algorithm)?
options: Use an operator stack with precedence rules: push operators, pop higher-precedence operators to output before pushing. Parentheses control scoping
quiz.explanation: Dijkstra's Shunting-yard: operator stack manages precedence. Higher-precedence operators on stack get popped before lower-precedence ones are pushed. Classic stack algorithm.

quiz.q: What's the truncation rule for division in this problem?
options: Truncate toward zero: 6/(-3) = -2, not -3. In Java, integer division already truncates toward zero. In Python, use int(a/b) not a//b
quiz.explanation: The problem specifies truncation toward zero. Java's / operator does this natively. Python's // floors (rounds toward -∞), so use int(a/b) for truncation toward zero. Language-specific gotcha.

quiz.q: How does this relate to how CPUs actually evaluate expressions?
options: CPUs use register-based or stack-based evaluation similar to RPN. The JVM is a stack machine that evaluates bytecode in essentially RPN order
quiz.explanation: The JVM and WebAssembly are stack machines. Bytecode instructions push/pop operands like RPN. Understanding RPN = understanding how your code actually executes at the VM level.

problems.title: Asteroid Collision
problems.tldr: Asteroids move in a row. Positive = right, negative = left. Same direction never collide. Opposite direction: larger survives, equal both explode. Use stack to simulate collisions.
problems.keyTrick: Stack holds surviving asteroids. For each new asteroid: if it's negative (moving left) and stack top is positive (moving right), they collide. Compare sizes in a while loop — the new asteroid may destroy multiple stack elements before being destroyed or surviving.

approaches.name: Stack Simulation
approaches.description: Push asteroids. When new negative meets positive top, resolve collision: pop smaller, both if equal. New asteroid may survive multiple collisions.

quiz.q: Why do only right-moving (positive) and left-moving (negative) asteroids collide?
options: Same direction = never catch each other (same speed). Two left-moving never collide with each other on the stack since they're already resolved. Only right-on-stack + left-incoming collide
quiz.explanation: Right-movers on the stack haven't hit anything yet. A new left-mover approaches them. Same direction: parallel paths, no collision. Two left-movers: both moving away from the stack.

quiz.q: What's the tricky case most people miss?
options: A small positive asteroid followed by a large negative one: the negative destroys the positive AND may continue to destroy more positives behind it. The while loop handles this chain reaction
quiz.explanation: Example: [5, 10, -11]. -11 destroys 10 (|-11|>10), then destroys 5 (|-11|>5). Result: [-11]. The while loop must continue checking until the new asteroid is destroyed or stack is empty/safe.

quiz.q: What's the loop termination condition?
options: The new asteroid is destroyed (matched or beaten), OR the stack is empty, OR the stack top is also moving left (no collision possible)
quiz.explanation: Three exit conditions: 1) new asteroid explodes (|new| ≤ |top|), 2) stack empty, 3) top is negative (same direction as new, no collision). Missing any condition = infinite loop or wrong result.

quiz.q: What's the time complexity despite nested loops?
options: O(n) — each asteroid is pushed at most once and popped at most once. Total push + pop operations ≤ 2n, so amortized O(n)
quiz.explanation: Classic amortized argument: each element enters and leaves the stack at most once. The inner while loop across all iterations does at most n total pops. Total work: O(n).

quiz.q: How would you extend this to 2D asteroid collisions?
options: 2D requires tracking positions and trajectories, using event-driven simulation with a priority queue. Fundamentally different from the 1D stack approach
quiz.explanation: 1D collision benefits from total ordering (left-to-right). 2D has no such ordering — you need computational geometry (sweep line, event queue). This shows why 1D constraints enable elegant solutions.

problems.title: Daily Temperatures
problems.tldr: For each day, find how many days until a warmer temperature. Monotonic decreasing stack of INDICES. When a warmer day arrives, pop all cooler days and record their wait time.
problems.keyTrick: Push indices (not values) onto a decreasing stack. When temp[i] > temp[stack.top()], pop and set answer[popped] = i - popped. This resolves the 'next warmer day' for every popped index. Stack stores indices of unresolved days.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.description: For each day, scan forward for first warmer day.

approaches.name: Monotonic Decreasing Stack
approaches.description: Stack of indices in decreasing temp order. Push current. Pop when current temp > stack top. Set answer on pop.

quiz.q: Why store indices on the stack instead of temperatures?
options: We need both the temperature (for comparison) and the index (for computing distance). Index gives both: temp = temps[index], distance = current_index - popped_index
quiz.explanation: Storing indices is strictly more informative: you can always look up temp[index], but you can't recover the index from a temperature (duplicates exist). Indices are the universal choice for monotonic stacks.

quiz.q: What invariant does the monotonic decreasing stack maintain?
options: All temperatures corresponding to stack indices are in non-increasing order from bottom to top. Each index on the stack is 'waiting' for a warmer day
quiz.explanation: Bottom-to-top: decreasing temperatures. Each stack element hasn't found its next warmer day yet. When a warmer day arrives, it resolves all cooler waiting days via pops.

quiz.q: Why is this O(n) despite nested loops (outer for + inner while)?
options: Each index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once. Total pushes + pops ≤ 2n. The while loop across ALL iterations of the for loop does at most n pops total
quiz.explanation: This is the canonical amortized O(n) argument for monotonic stacks. Each of n elements enters and exits the stack exactly once. Total work across all while-loop iterations = n pops.

quiz.q: What does a remaining non-empty stack at the end mean?
options: Those indices never found a warmer day — their answer stays 0 (default). No special handling needed if answer array is initialized to 0
quiz.explanation: Leftover stack elements had no subsequent warmer day. Their answer[i] = 0 by default. This is why we initialize the answer array with zeros. Clean handling of the edge case.

quiz.q: Name three other problems that use the same monotonic stack pattern:
options: Next Greater Element, Stock Span, Largest Rectangle in Histogram — all use 'next greater/smaller' queries resolved by monotonic stack
quiz.explanation: Monotonic stack is a meta-pattern: any 'for each element, find the next/previous greater/smaller element' is O(n) with a monotonic stack. Recognizing this pattern is essential.

problems.title: Online Stock Span
problems.tldr: For each day's price, return the span: count of consecutive days before (including today) where price was ≤ today's. Monotonic decreasing stack of (price, span) pairs.
problems.keyTrick: Stack stores (price, span) pairs in decreasing price order. When new price ≥ stack top price, pop and ACCUMULATE the popped span into current span. Push (price, accumulated_span). The span carries forward collapsed information.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.complexity: O(n) per call, O(n) total space
approaches.description: Store all prices. For each call, scan backward counting consecutive ≤ days.

approaches.name: Monotonic Stack with Span Accumulation
approaches.complexity: O(1) amortized per call, O(n) space
approaches.description: Stack of (price, span) pairs. Pop and accumulate spans when current price ≥ top. Push accumulated result.

quiz.q: Why accumulate spans instead of just counting pops?
options: Popped elements may themselves represent multiple days (their own accumulated span). Adding their span captures ALL the days they represent, not just the single pop
quiz.explanation: A popped (price=50, span=3) represents 3 consecutive days where price ≤ 50. When we pop it for price=60, those 3 days also have price ≤ 60. Must add 3, not 1.

quiz.q: How does this relate to 'Previous Greater Element' problem?
options: Stock span = index - index_of_previous_greater_element. The monotonic stack finds the previous greater element. Span is the distance to it
quiz.explanation: Span(i) = i - prevGreater(i). The stack maintains a decreasing sequence; the first element that stays is the previous greater. All problems in the 'next/previous greater/smaller' family are equivalent.

quiz.q: What's the worst-case space usage?
options: O(n) when prices are strictly decreasing — nothing ever gets popped. Every element stays on the stack
quiz.explanation: Strictly decreasing prices: [100, 90, 80, 70...]. No element pops any other. Stack grows to size n. This is the worst case. Best case (increasing): stack stays size 1.

quiz.q: This is an 'online' algorithm. What does that mean?
options: It processes elements one at a time as they arrive, without needing access to future elements. Suitable for streaming data
It processes all data at once
It needs the full array upfront
quiz.explanation: Online = streaming. Each call to next() processes one price and returns immediately. No need to know future prices. Contrast with 'offline' where all data is available upfront.

quiz.q: How would you implement this for a sliding window of size k (last k days only)?
options: Maintain the monotonic stack but also track ages of entries. When an entry becomes older than k days, it must be removed even if not popped naturally. Requires a deque
quiz.explanation: Sliding window + monotonic stack = monotonic deque. Elements are removed from both ends: front (too old) and back (smaller than new). This is the Sliding Window Maximum pattern.

problems.title: Car Fleet
problems.tldr: Cars at different positions/speeds drive toward a target. A faster car behind a slower one merges into a fleet. Count the number of fleets that arrive. Sort by position descending, use stack to track arrival times.
problems.keyTrick: Sort by position (closest to target first). For each car, compute arrival time = (target - pos) / speed. Push arrival time onto stack. If current car's time ≤ stack top (it catches the car ahead), it joins that fleet — don't push. Otherwise, it forms a new fleet — push.

approaches.name: Sort + Stack
approaches.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
approaches.description: Sort by position descending. Compute arrival times. Stack tracks fleet leaders: push only if arrival time > stack top.

approaches.name: Sort + Simple Comparison
approaches.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space
approaches.description: Sort by position descending. Track current fleet's arrival time. Count new fleets when arrival time exceeds current.

quiz.q: Why sort by position descending (closest to target first)?
options: Processing from front to back: if a car behind arrives earlier than the car ahead, it's blocked and merges. We need to know the 'wall' (slower car ahead) before processing faster cars behind
quiz.explanation: The car closest to target sets the 'speed limit' for all cars behind it that would catch up. Processing front-to-back lets us establish these limits before encountering faster cars.

quiz.q: Why is arrival time = (target - position) / speed sufficient?
options: Without blocking, each car's solo arrival time is (target-pos)/speed. If this time ≤ the fleet ahead's time, it catches up and merges. Merging doesn't change the fleet's arrival time
Need to simulate step by step
quiz.explanation: A fleet travels at the speed of its slowest member (the leader). A faster car that catches the fleet adopts the fleet's arrival time. So we only compare solo times with the current fleet leader.

quiz.q: What's the subtle reason we use floating-point division here?
options: Integer division would truncate arrival times, causing incorrect ordering. (target-pos)/speed must be exact to correctly determine which cars catch which fleets
quiz.explanation: Consider: (10-5)/3 = 1.667 vs (10-2)/4 = 2.0. With integer division: 1 vs 2. With float: 1.667 vs 2.0. The ordering is the same here but edge cases differ. Use doubles.

quiz.q: If two cars have the same arrival time, what happens?
options: They form one fleet — the behind car catches the ahead car exactly at the target. Equal arrival time means they merge
quiz.explanation: Same arrival time = they meet at the target line. Per the problem, they merge into one fleet. This is why the condition is ≤ (not strictly <) for merging.

quiz.q: How does this problem demonstrate the power of problem transformation?
options: The physical simulation (positions, speeds, time) is transformed into a simple stack problem on arrival times. The key insight is finding the right representation to simplify the problem
The stack is the hard part
quiz.explanation: Direct simulation is O(n²) or complex. Converting to arrival times reduces it to 'count distinct decreasing segments' — a simple stack problem. Finding the right transformation is the core skill.

problems.title: Simplify Path
problems.tldr: Simplify a Unix-style file path. Split by '/', use stack: push directory names, pop on '..', ignore '.' and empty strings. Join stack with '/' for result.
problems.keyTrick: Split by '/'. Filter tokens: skip empty strings and '.'. On '..', pop (go up one directory) if stack is non-empty. Push everything else (directory names). Result = '/' + stack joined by '/'.

approaches.name: Stack + Split
approaches.description: Split path by '/'. Process each token with stack: push names, pop on '..', skip '.' and empty. Join result.

quiz.q: Why split by '/' first instead of character-by-character processing?
options: Splitting handles consecutive slashes ('///') automatically — they produce empty strings which are filtered. Character-by-character requires manual slash-tracking
quiz.explanation: '/a///b/../c' splits to ['', 'a', '', '', 'b', '..', 'c']. Empty strings from consecutive slashes are easily filtered. Character processing needs a state machine for the same result.

quiz.q: What should happen when '..' is encountered with an empty stack (already at root)?
options: Do nothing — you can't go above root. '/../../' simplifies to '/'. The stack stays empty
quiz.explanation: In Unix, cd .. at root stays at root. The simplified path can't go above /. So '..' with empty stack is a no-op. This edge case is commonly missed.

quiz.q: What are the only tokens that modify the stack?
options: Directory names (push) and '..' (pop). Everything else is ignored: '.' (current dir), empty strings (consecutive slashes), and trailing slashes
quiz.explanation: Two actions only: push (new directory) and pop (..). All other tokens are noise. This clean separation makes the algorithm simple and correct.

quiz.q: How does this relate to how operating systems actually resolve paths?
options: OS path resolution uses essentially this algorithm. Additional considerations: symlinks, permissions, and mount points add complexity but the core logic is stack-based
OS uses a completely different method
quiz.explanation: The Linux kernel's path resolution (path_lookup) processes components left-to-right, following '..' by going to parent. Same stack logic with additional filesystem checks. This is real systems programming.

quiz.q: What if '...' (three dots) appears in the path?
options: It's treated as a regular directory name and pushed onto the stack. Only exactly '..' has special meaning, not '...' or '....'
quiz.explanation: '...' is a valid directory name (unusual but legal in Unix). Only '.' and '..' have special meanings. This edge case tests careful reading of the problem constraints.

problems.title: Decode String
problems.tldr: Decode encoded string: '3[a2[c]]' → 'accaccacc'. Use stack: push current string and repeat count on '['. On ']', pop and construct repeated string. Handle nested brackets naturally.
problems.keyTrick: Two-item stack frame: (currentString, repeatCount). On '[': push current state and reset. On ']': pop previous state, append current string × count to previous string. Digits may be multi-digit — accumulate them.

approaches.name: Stack with State Frames
approaches.complexity: O(maxK^depth × n) time, O(sum of decoded lengths) space
approaches.description: Push (string, count) on '['. Pop on ']' and construct. Handle multi-digit numbers.

approaches.name: Recursion
approaches.description: Recursive descent: parse number, expect '[', recurse for content, expect ']'. Cleaner but uses call stack.

quiz.q: Why are two separate stacks (or a stack of pairs) needed?
options: On '[', we need to save BOTH the string built so far AND the repeat count. On ']', we combine: previous_string + current_string × count. Both pieces of state must be preserved
quiz.explanation: The string-so-far and the repeat count are both context that must be saved/restored on bracket entry/exit. It's like saving registers on a function call — same concept.

quiz.q: How do you handle multi-digit numbers like '100[a]'?
options: Accumulate digits: when you see a digit character, multiply running number by 10 and add digit. Reset on '[' after pushing
Use Integer.parseInt on the whole string
quiz.explanation: Build number digit by digit: num = num * 10 + (c - '0'). When '[' is encountered, the accumulated number is the repeat count. Reset number to 0 after pushing.

quiz.q: What makes the recursive approach more natural for this problem?
options: The string has recursive structure (brackets inside brackets). Recursive descent parsing directly mirrors this nesting. The stack approach is simulating the recursion explicitly
quiz.explanation: The encoded string is essentially a recursive grammar: string = chars | number '[' string ']'. Recursive descent directly parses this grammar. The stack approach is the iterative equivalent.

quiz.q: What's the time complexity and why is it hard to analyze?
options: The output string can be exponentially long: '2[2[2[a]]]' = 'aaaaaaaa' (length 8 from input length 11). Time/space is O(output length), which depends on nesting depth and repeat counts
quiz.explanation: The output can be exponentially larger than input. Time is O(|output|) since every character must be produced. This is one of few problems where output size dominates input size in complexity.

quiz.q: How does this pattern appear in real-world systems?
options: Template expansion in config files, macro expansion in preprocessors, and compression schemes like run-length encoding all use recursive decode patterns
quiz.explanation: Template engines (Jinja, Mustache), C preprocessor macro expansion, and decompression algorithms all recursively expand encoded representations. This is a fundamental parsing pattern.

problems.title: Maximum Frequency Stack
problems.tldr: Design FreqStack: push adds element, pop removes the most frequent element (ties broken by most recent). Use frequency map + map of stacks per frequency + track maxFreq.
problems.keyTrick: Three structures: 1) freq{} maps value→frequency, 2) freqToStack{} maps frequency→stack of values at that frequency, 3) maxFreq tracks current maximum. Push: increment freq, push to freqToStack[newFreq], update maxFreq. Pop: pop from freqToStack[maxFreq], decrement freq, shrink maxFreq if stack empty.

approaches.name: Frequency Map + Frequency-Indexed Stacks
approaches.complexity: O(1) push and pop, O(n) space
approaches.description: Map values to frequencies. Map frequencies to stacks. Track maxFreq. Push/pop update all three structures in O(1).

quiz.q: Why does each frequency level need its OWN stack (not a single sorted structure)?
options: Each frequency stack maintains insertion order within that frequency level, giving LIFO for tie-breaking. A sorted structure would lose this temporal ordering
quiz.explanation: The problem requires popping the most frequent, with ties broken by most recently pushed. Separate stacks per frequency preserve push-order within each frequency level. LIFO tie-breaking is automatic.

quiz.q: Why can maxFreq only decrease by 1 when we pop?
options: We pop one occurrence from the maxFreq stack. This decreases that value's frequency by 1. If the stack at maxFreq becomes empty, the next highest frequency is maxFreq-1 (which is guaranteed non-empty)
quiz.explanation: When we push, we add to freq f AND freq f-1 (and all lower) stacks. So freqToStack[maxFreq-1] always has at least the elements that were in freqToStack[maxFreq] minus the popped one. It's never empty.

quiz.q: Wait — do elements appear in multiple frequency stacks simultaneously?
options: Yes! When we push 'a' three times, 'a' appears in freqToStack[1], freqToStack[2], AND freqToStack[3]. Each push adds to the NEW frequency's stack without removing from old ones
quiz.explanation: This is the non-obvious insight. 'a' pushed 3 times: it's in freq[1], freq[2], freq[3]. When popped from freq[3], it still exists in freq[2]. This is why the approach works without cleanup.

quiz.q: What's the space complexity and can it be optimized?
options: O(n) where n = total pushes. Each push adds one entry to a frequency stack. No optimization possible since all entries may be needed
quiz.explanation: Each push adds one stack entry. Total entries = total pushes = n. The freq map and freqToStack map are both bounded by n. Space is Θ(n) and can't be reduced.

quiz.q: How would you extend this to popMin frequency (least frequent, ties by oldest)?
options: Track minFreq similarly. But minFreq is harder — it can jump unpredictably when frequencies change. Need to find next non-empty frequency level, possibly requiring a TreeMap or ordered set
Same approach, just pop from minFreq
quiz.explanation: maxFreq only moves ±1, making it O(1) to maintain. minFreq can jump arbitrarily (e.g., if the only freq-1 element gets a second push). Finding new min requires O(log n) with TreeMap.

problems.title: Largest Rectangle In Histogram
problems.tldr: Find the largest rectangle in a histogram. For each bar, find how far it extends left and right (until a shorter bar). Monotonic increasing stack: on smaller bar, pop and compute area using popped height × (right - left - 1).
problems.keyTrick: Monotonic INCREASING stack of indices. When heights[i] < heights[stack.top()], pop: the popped bar's height is the rectangle height. Width = i - stack.peek() - 1 (or i if stack is empty). This computes the max rectangle for each bar as its height.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.description: For each bar, expand left and right to find max rectangle with that bar as the shortest.

approaches.name: Monotonic Increasing Stack
approaches.description: Push indices while heights increase. On decrease, pop and compute area. Handle remaining stack at end.

approaches.name: Divide and Conquer
approaches.complexity: O(n log n) avg, O(n²) worst
approaches.description: Find min bar, max rectangle = max(min×width, left half, right half). O(n²) worst case without segment tree.

quiz.q: When we pop index j because heights[i] < heights[j], what is the width of the rectangle with height heights[j]?
options: Width = i - stack.peek() - 1. The left boundary is the index below j on the stack (the previous shorter bar). Right boundary is i. If stack is empty, width = i
quiz.explanation: The popped bar j's rectangle extends from the bar after stack.peek() to the bar before i. Width = i - stack.peek() - 1. If stack is empty after pop, it extends to index 0, so width = i.

quiz.q: Why use an INCREASING stack (not decreasing like Daily Temperatures)?
options: We want the 'previous smaller' and 'next smaller' elements for each bar. An increasing stack: push while heights increase, pop on smaller — the pop tells us both boundaries of the rectangle
quiz.explanation: Increasing stack ensures each pop is triggered by a SMALLER bar (right boundary). The element below on the stack is the previous SMALLER bar (left boundary). Both boundaries found simultaneously.

quiz.q: What happens to elements remaining on the stack after processing all bars?
options: They have no smaller bar to the right. Pop each one: right boundary = n (end of array). Width = n - stack.peek() - 1 (or n if stack becomes empty)
quiz.explanation: Remaining bars extend all the way to the right edge. Use n as the right boundary. This 'cleanup' phase is often forgotten. Some solutions add a sentinel height 0 at the end to trigger all remaining pops.

quiz.q: The sentinel trick (appending height 0) eliminates which edge case?
options: The cleanup phase for remaining stack elements. Height 0 is smaller than everything, forcing all remaining elements to pop. No separate cleanup loop needed
quiz.explanation: Appending 0 at the end: all remaining stack elements are popped during the main loop (since 0 < any positive height). Cleaner code with one loop instead of two. A common implementation trick.

quiz.q: How does this directly connect to 'Maximal Rectangle' in a binary matrix?
options: Treat each row as the base of a histogram: height[j] = consecutive 1s above including current row. Run Largest Rectangle for each row. O(m×n) total
quiz.explanation: Maximal Rectangle (LC 85) builds histograms row by row and runs this algorithm on each. O(m×n). This is a classic problem decomposition: reduce 2D to repeated 1D. Google favorite.
